```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(RdistNN)
```

This walkthrough fits conditional average treatment effects (CATE) and
conditional means at selected covariate profiles. Install the package using
the [README](https://github.com/JakobJuergens/RdistNN#installation).
Use `browseVignettes("RdistNN")` to open the installed guide collection.
The [paper](https://jakobjuergens.com/research/#orthogonal-inference-conditional-z)
gives the statistical assumptions and results; this guide covers the calls
and how to read their outputs.

Use `x0` for one profile or `X0` for a matrix with one profile per row.
Covariates and supplied predictions must be finite, complete and aligned in
the same observation order. Data-frame targets follow the `x_cols` order.

## Conditional average treatment effects

For binary treatment `D`, the AIPW inputs are outcome `Y`, control and treated
conditional means `m0` and `m1`, and propensity `e`. Nuisance fitting is external
to the package. This simulation supplies **oracle nuisances** so that the
example demonstrates localization without choosing a nuisance learner.

```{r cate}
demo_cate <- cate_demo_data(n = 180, p = 2, design = "hetero", seed = 1)
df <- demo_cate$data

fit_cate <- cate_dnn(
  data = df, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y", t_col = "D",
  m0_col = "m0_oracle", m1_col = "m1_oracle", e_col = "e_oracle",
  x0 = c(0, 0), k = 1L, se = TRUE,
  return = c("W", "dx", "psi")
)

summary(fit_cate)
confint(fit_cate)
predict(fit_cate, x0 = c(0.2, -0.1), interval = "confidence")
```

`fit_cate$tau` contains the estimates and `fit_cate$se` contains their
jackknife standard errors. `nobs(fit_cate)` counts training observations;
local effective sample size describes weight concentration. `confint()`
returns pointwise normal intervals, not simultaneous confidence bands.

If you already have an observation-level pseudo-outcome, pass it directly.
Here we use the aligned oracle AIPW column from the same demo data:

```{r cate-matrix}
X <- as.matrix(df[c("X1", "X2")])
fit_cate_matrix <- cate_dnn(
  X = X, x0 = c(0, 0), pseudo_outcome = df$aipw_oracle, k = 1L
)

c(data_frame = fit_cate$tau, matrix = fit_cate_matrix$tau)
```

The data-frame pathway also accepts `pseudo_outcome`. See `?cate_dnn` for the
complete input contract. Preserve the same observation order for every
nuisance or pseudo-outcome vector.

### Migrating earlier CATE inputs

The normalized Robinson construction has been removed. Replace earlier `m_col`
calls with propensity and both arm-specific outcome means for AIPW, or supply
an externally justified signal through `pseudo_outcome`. A pooled outcome mean
is not a substitute for the two arm means. Demo data now include `m1_oracle`
and `aipw_oracle`; the former `rho_oracle` used a different signal, so this is
not a numerically equivalent column rename.

Fresh nuisance-based fitting constructs
`mu1 - mu0 + D*(Y-mu1)/e - (1-D)*(Y-mu0)/(1-e)`, with validated and clipped
propensities. The retired `m_col` argument remains rejected. A directly supplied
`pseudo_outcome` takes precedence over accompanying nuisance selectors and is
localized unchanged; its construction, causal interpretation and inferential
justification remain the caller's responsibility. The paper's residualized-slope
estimating equation is distinct from the removed normalized pseudo-outcome.

Each new fit records `meta$signal_source`: `"aipw"` means the package constructed
the signal through its nuisance-input branch, and `"supplied"` means the caller
provided it. A supplied vector remains `"supplied"` even when it equals AIPW or
comes from a column named `aipw_oracle`. `meta$created_with_version` records the
version of the package actually loaded when the original fit was created.
Candidate views and summaries preserve that version. Neither field certifies
identification, same-sample nuisance accuracy or stability, localization bias,
or the conditions for pointwise inference.

Refit objects created by older development versions. Both packages reuse
current fitted state for prediction, covariance, candidates and diagnostics;
they do not reconstruct retired object schemas or score methods. Prediction
returns ordinary numeric vectors, matrices or `list(fit, se.fit)`.
See the companion's
[saved-fit guide](https://github.com/JakobJuergens/RdistNN_stata/blob/master/docs/reusing-fits.md).

### Covariance between prespecified profiles

```{r cate-covariance}
profiles <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(0.2, -0.1))
joint <- cate_dnn(X = X, X0 = profiles, pseudo_outcome = df$aipw_oracle,
                 s = fit_cate$meta$s, return = character())
V <- vcov(joint)
a <- c(1, -1)
c(contrast = sum(a * coef(joint)),
  contrast_se = sqrt(drop(crossprod(a, V %*% a))))
```

Both covariance axes follow `coef(joint)`. Common deleted observations retain
dependence between profiles. Valid contrast inference requires the relevant
joint assumptions; pointwise intervals alone do not establish it.

The documented sampling framework uses independent observations and supplies
neither cluster nor survey-design inference. At each target, observations with
exactly equal represented distance under the selected metric share the mean
of their assigned rank weights, including each deletion's surviving group.
No tolerance merges nearby distances, and signals/nuisances do not define groups.
Aligned row permutations preserve estimates and covariance up to numerical
precision. Individual weights, support and ESS can change. The paper assumes
a continuous distance distribution, under which old and new policies agree
almost surely; inference with persistent distance ties is not established.
The reported `s/n` is descriptive, not a calibrated inference threshold.

### Check local support

Supplied propensities must lie in `[0, 1]`; AIPW uses clipped values with
`clip = 1e-8` by default. Clipping prevents undefined denominators but cannot
create local treatment support. Supplied pseudo-outcomes are used unchanged.

Inspect local weight concentration and treated/control mass:

```{r cate-diagnostics}
d_cate <- as.data.frame(diagnostics(fit_cate))
d_cate[, c("target_id", "n_eff", "treated_mass", "control_mass")]
```

Diagnostics describe the realized sample near a target; they are not a test
of the paper's assumptions. Keep `"W"` in `return` for weight diagnostics,
`"dx"` for metric-distance summaries. Overlap remains available from the
supplied treatment/propensity inputs without requesting a `"nuisance"` extra.

## Nonparametric regression

`np_dnn()` estimates a conditional mean. Regression fits support the same
`summary()`, `coef()`, `confint()`, `vcov()`, `nobs()` and `predict()` calls as CATE;
their direct estimate and standard-error fields are `mu` and `se`.

```{r regression}
demo_np <- np_demo_data(n = 160, p = 2, design = "sinusoidal", seed = 2)
fit_np <- np_dnn(
  data = demo_np$data, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y",
  X0 = rbind(c(0, 0), c(0.5, 0)), k = 1L, se = TRUE,
  return = c("W", "dx", "ess")
)

summary(fit_np)$coefficients
confint(fit_np)
predict(fit_np, x0 = c(0.2, -0.1), interval = "confidence")
```

Use uppercase `Y` for the matrix interface:

```{r regression-matrix}
fit_np_matrix <- np_dnn(
  X = as.matrix(demo_np$data[c("X1", "X2")]),
  Y = demo_np$data$Y, x0 = c(0, 0), k = 1L
)
fit_np_matrix$mu
```

`predict()` evaluates new profiles using the retained training outcomes and
geometry. Two-scale regression uses `np_tdnn()` with orders `s1 < s2` and
`s2 < n` for jackknife uncertainty. See `?np_tdnn` for its signed weights and
additional requirements.

## Choosing localization and uncertainty settings

The defaults use exact DNN weights and `k = 1`. Unless `s` or `tuning` is
supplied, the subsample order is
`s = floor(0.4 * n^((p + 1)/(p + 2)))`, where `p` is the covariate dimension.
Larger `s` concentrates more weight near the target. The written manuscript
derivations use `k = 1`; larger fixed `k` is supported in the implementation.

The order `s` is not a count of observations retained in a nearest-neighbor
truncation. The unaveraged exact rank table has support through rank
`n - s + k` (`n - s + 1` for `k = 1`). Block averaging can extend nonzero
observation weights to the end of an exact-distance group crossing that
edge. The optional `neighbors`
extra reports the first `k` neighbors, rather than the full weight support.

For sensitivity analysis, compare the paper's candidate orders without
changing the primary result:

```{r tuning}
fit_grid <- np_dnn(
  data = demo_np$data, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y",
  x0 = c(0, 0), tuning_mode = "grid", se = FALSE
)
fit_grid$tuning_grid$candidates
candidate_fit(fit_grid, 1L)$mu
```

`tuning_dnn_paper()` uses `lambda = 0.4` and the grid
`c(0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.75)`; `s` is recomputed for each candidate.
Grid mode is a sensitivity comparison, not an automatic optimization rule.
It cannot be combined with explicit `s`.

For uncertainty, `jackknife = "fast"` reuses full-sample ranks;
`jackknife = "loo"` directly recomputes leave-one-out weights. Delete-1
inference requires `s < n`. Set `se = FALSE` to omit standard errors.

## Seeds and native threads

Built-in distance, rank-weight and accumulation calculations are deterministic:
both R and C++ preserve an existing RNG state and leave `.Random.seed` absent
when it was absent. These calculations need no seed.

The demo helpers' explicit `seed` arguments restore the caller's saved RNG
state. `seed = NULL` draws from the current stream. Simulation grids use
`master_seed` to generate their replicate seeds. To reproduce a grid, also retain
the RNG kind, dependency versions and availability, future plan and tuning
configuration; equal integer seeds alone do not guarantee agreement between
the `future.apply` route and its fallback. See `?sim_cate_run` for the
reproducibility contract shared with `sim_iv_run()`.

Eligible calculations use C++ automatically when their native routine is
available. For engine comparisons or troubleshooting,
`options(RdistNN.use_compiled = FALSE)` selects the package's R paths;
`options(RdistNN.use_compiled = TRUE)` restores automatic native dispatch.
Source installation still requires a C++17 compiler. A native execution error
stops the calculation rather than silently retrying it in R. During a long
native calculation, interruption can be delayed until control returns to R.

Native routines default to at most two OpenMP threads. Set
`options(RdistNN.num_threads = 4L)` to request four, or `1L` for one native
thread. Lower OpenMP runtime limits still apply. See `?RdistNN` for the
controls and saved-RNG-state limitations.

## Plots and reusable weights

Plotting is optional and requires ggplot2. Dashboards additionally require
patchwork. Both fitted workflows support the estimate and weight views:

```{r plots, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5}
plot(fit_np)
plot_weights(fit_cate, type = "profile")
```

For your own scalar signal, build weights directly. Rows of `W` index
observations and columns index target points:

```{r weights}
wt <- weights_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = rbind(c(0, 0), c(0.5, 0)), k = 1L, s = 12L,
  return = "W"
)
dim(wt$W)
as.vector(crossprod(wt$W, fit_cate$psi))
```
